title: Claire Hearthford
type: Herbalist and mother · early Pristinian adventurer
dek: A mother who ventures out because people need care, then helps make a stable town in which her daughter can live, learn and form friendships.

facts.Work: Medicinal herbs, alchemy and practical care
facts.Open record: Katherine’s condition is described by Claire; no completed cure or later family fate is established

body:
Claire Hearthford does not introduce herself as a soldier. She joins the early expeditions because someone may be injured, while making arrangements for her daughter Katherine to remain safely in town. Protecting a future for her child is the center of a wider willingness to care for other people.

Going because someone may need help

Before leaving town, Claire asks who can look after her daughter. On the journey she talks with Gartina about kitchen work and Katherine’s love of potatoes, ordinary concerns that sit beside the danger the company is entering.

When undead and an animated tree attack, she notices the limits of her arrows and suggests other means of striking the wood. She warns the others about an undead creature slipping close and shoots it over Gartina. She can act under pressure while still wanting the outing over so she can return to Katherine.

Work that leaves room for her daughter

When Pristinia discusses building and defense, Claire offers what she actually knows. She is neither a carpenter nor an expert wilderness guide, but has experience with medicinal herbs and alchemy. Work based in town would let her contribute and keep an eye on Katherine.

Even that expertise has limits. She recognizes herbs as prepared medicines more readily than she can identify every raw plant. She wants supplies labeled for whoever must use them next and declines to experiment with something beyond her present skill. Her practicality depends on admitting the difference between having experience and being able to do everything.

A future longer than her own

Claire says Katherine has a hereditary condition from her father’s side and worries about fever when the child becomes excited. She hopes an elven doctor might understand it better. Her promise that they will find a way to help is a mother’s hope; the scenes do not establish a diagnosis or cure.

Her concern extends beyond keeping Katherine still and safe. She wants her daughter to make friends and refuses the idea that a longer lifespan makes human friendships pointless. Friends can have children and grandchildren; a life can remain connected across generations. Claire also knows she will not always be present to do everything for her daughter.

Someone who cannot afford a glorious death

A later encounter leaves Claire wary of beings who say they were controlled. She wonders where responsibility lies if a person is made to commit a crime, then tries to leave as the threat grows. She rushes to examine companions in distress but argues against remaining where they cannot help.

She says some people cannot afford to die heroes yet. With Katherine’s needs already established, the line has a concrete cost behind it. Seeking retreat and bringing injured people toward town are part of care, not proof that she has ceased to answer danger.

Remembering the people still here

As another attempt to help reaches its limit, Claire listens to a warning about making a dangerous mistake. The magic on display is beyond anything she pretends to command. When the effort ends, she says they must continue caring for the living.

Her place in the early Vanguard tradition rests on that repeated work: joining expeditions, using the skills she has, asking for help where she lacks it and trying to make the settlement livable for people who cannot simply spend their lives at the front. The selected record does not supply the family’s later departure or final fate.
